overview: This entry covers Kenya under British colonial rule, especially the 1920s and 1930s. The colony and the coastal protectorate had different legal arrangements. Railways, towns and schools changed opportunities, but racial restrictions on land, movement and political power made those changes deeply unequal.

periods.title: Protectorate and railway expansion
periods.summary: The railway reached Nairobi in 1899 and Kisumu in 1901, before this entry’s main interval.

periods.title: Colony, towns and organized demands
periods.summary: Colonial Kenya combined new transport and schooling with racial restrictions and growing African political organization.

periods.title: Later struggle and independence
periods.summary: The imported endpoint is not the end of British rule, which lasted until December 1963.

items.text: The railway reached Nairobi in 1899 and the lakeside terminus later named Kisumu in 1901. Transport infrastructure helped towns grow along the line. These dates describe the network inherited by people living in the 1920s, not new construction in the selected year.

Indian workers and African labourers helped construct the railway, and some Indian workers also opened small shops. Rail history therefore includes migration, commerce and difficult labour, alongside engineering plans drawn by British officials.

The Smithsonian preserves a thin tin kipande case made in the 1920s, with loops for a neck chain. It once held folded employment papers dated 1925. An object small enough to wear could carry a government’s authority into a worker’s daily movements.

The papers in a kipande recorded an African owner’s name and work history and rules restricting movement. This specimen was collected much later, in 1986. Its museum arrival is not the date when the colonial identification system was used.

sections.title: A house, a family and a school

items.text: Colonial authorities restricted African ownership of urban land. Some employers provided only bachelor rooms for workers, making it difficult for families to settle together. Housing policy shaped who could live in a town, not merely how buildings looked.

Asian residents also faced restrictions on property ownership and representation, while some Nairobi neighbourhoods were demolished under public-health justifications. Historians describe African and Asian resistance to these policies; residents were not passive recipients of town planning.

Alliance School opened near Nairobi in 1926 under Protestant missions. By 1928 it offered a four-year secondary course and the Cambridge School Certificate. Schooling could become a route toward professional work, although access remained highly limited and unequal.

Earlier, Maseno pupils had demanded more than gardening, carpentry and hygiene instruction. A 1910 strike helped secure teaching in English, mathematics and geography. This background shows pupils themselves pressing to change what colonial-era education allowed them to learn.

During the 1930s, Kikuyu independent schools drew on donated land, elected committees and community fundraising. Families helped create institutions when existing education did not meet their aspirations. Choosing a school could also express a position in religious and political debates.

sections.title: A newspaper sample and money in circulation

items.text: “Muigwithania”, meaning “The Reconciler”, is the Kikuyu title of the newspaper associated with the Kikuyu Central Association and Jomo Kenyatta. Surviving 1928 and 1929 issues preserve the language in the Latin alphabet. This sample follows the catalogue’s spelling.

The same newspaper collection includes English translations and correspondence between colonial officials. Those documents preserve African arguments against colonial rule, but they also show how the state watched the press. An archive can record both a voice and the surveillance directed at it.

Regional money changed from rupees through an intermediate florin to shillings and cents. The currency transition linked everyday purchases to decisions made by the East African Currency Board. Older and newer names for money could coexist while people adjusted.

ending.text: British rule ended when Kenya became independent on 12 December 1963; it became a republic the following year. The 1938 map endpoint does not mark independence. Colonial institutions changed, while the people who had lived, worked and organized under them continued building their country.
